extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of formal logic / philosophy (undergraduate/graduate)
extracted.subtask_description: Analyze, classify, and determine the import (meaning and truth-conditions) of verbal propositions in formal logic, distinguishing grammatical form from logical import. Covers copula/“to be” ambiguity, affirmation/negation, modality, complexity, quantification, distribution, and the role of connotation versus denotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double meaning of the copula ('to be')
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that the words 'to be' have a double meaning: (a) to exist, and (b) to be some specified thing (e.g. to be a man, to be Socrates, to be seen).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume a single idea underlies both uses of 'to be'; conflating existence and predication produces ambiguities and futile speculation. The historical failures in metaphysics often trace to overlooking this double meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affirmative vs Negative propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions divide into affirmative (predicate affirmed of the subject) and negative (predicate denied of the subject). The copula expresses affirmation ('is') or negation ('is not').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some logicians attempt to treat negation as part of the predicate (e.g., 'not-dead' as predicate), but this is largely a merely verbal simplification that obscures the real distinction between asserting presence and asserting absence. Prefer treating denial as distinct operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal/modal modifications attach to the copula
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences of tense/time (past/present/future) and certain modal forms (e.g. may, perhaps, it is possible) are properly considered as attaching to the copula (the sign of predication), not to the predicate itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time affects the applicability of the predicate to the subject (the event asserted), whereas modal expressions like 'may be' often indicate the state of our mind (absence of disbelief) rather than properties of the fact itself. Treat these as circumstances of predication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple vs Complex propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: A simple proposition affirms or denies one predicate of one subject. A complex proposition involves more than one predicate or more than one subject (or both).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many 'complex' propositions are in fact multiple distinct propositions joined by conjunctions; such conjunctions are often abbreviations of several propositions. Distinguish true complex forms (e.g., conditional/disjunctive where the assertion concerns relations among propositions) from mere aggregates of separate assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothetical/Conditional, Disjunctive, and Categorical propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypothetical/conditional propositions assert an inferential relation between propositions (e.g., 'If A then B'); disjunctive propositions ('Either A or B') are resolvable into conditional forms; categorical propositions assert without dependence on a condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that in hypotheticals the subject and predicate are names of propositions (the assertion is about propositions themselves). Particles like 'if', 'or', 'and' function as abbreviations indicating relations among propositions rather than adding ordinary predicates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal, Particular, Indefinite, and Singular propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification based on the degree of generality of the subject: Universal (predicate of all denoted), Particular (predicate of some non-assignable portion), Indefinite (form does not show whether universal or particular), Singular (subject is an individual name).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use context and custom of speech to resolve indeterminate cases. Examples: 'All men are mortal' (universal); 'Some men are wise' (particular); 'Man is mortal' often intended universal though form indefinite; 'Julius Caesar is mortal' (singular).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of terms
rubrics_metrics.description: A general name is distributed when it stands for each and every individual it denotes. Universal propositions have distributed subjects; particular propositions have undistributed subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether subject or predicate is being asserted of every member of the class. Use distribution terminology for concise statement of syllogistic rules (e.g., in 'All men are mortal' the subject 'man' is distributed; in 'Some men are mortal' both subject and predicate are undistributed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Particles as abbreviations (role of conjunctions and connectives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Words like 'and', 'but', 'or', 'if' are largely abbreviations or shorthand that compress entire propositions or relations among propositions into shorter forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing a sentence, expand such particles to their full propositional content to see whether it expresses multiple separate assertions or a single assertion about propositions (e.g., conditional). This helps detect when apparent complexity is an aggregation versus a true complex assertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish the import of propositions from the act of judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic should analyze the content (what is believed) — the things or facts — rather than the psychological act of believing or judging. Propositions express facts about things, not about our ideas of things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When determining truth-conditions and meaning, focus on the external phenomena the proposition asserts (e.g., 'fire causes heat' concerns natural phenomena), not on mental processes or the conjunction of ideas. Psychological analysis of judgment is a different inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hobbes' (denotation-based) account of predication — scope and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Hobbes analyzed propositions as the speaker's belief that the predicate is 'a name of the same thing' as the subject (i.e., a relation of denotation). This account is sufficient only where both terms are proper names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize Hobbes' account as capturing a fragment of propositional meaning (useful for identity-like predications) but inadequate for connotative/general names; do not reduce all predication to mere coincidence of denotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connotation (attributes) as the primary source of meaning for connotative names
rubrics_metrics.description: Except for proper names and non-connotative abstracts, the meaning of names resides in their connotation — the attributes they connote — and truth depends on the presence/absence of those attributes, not merely on denotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze propositions with connotative terms by examining the attributes implied by the terms (e.g., 'man' connotes certain attributes; 'mortal' connotes an attribute). The proposition 'All men are mortal' means: all objects possessing attributes connoted by 'man' also possess attributes connoted by 'mortal'. Connotative names follow from attributes — do not treat names as primary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form (collocation of words) underdetermines propositional meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere collocation of two names with a copula does not exhaust the meaning of a proposition; the same grammatical form can combine with other circumstances to yield much more content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not take logical form alone as a full account of import; attend to additional circumstances (context, connotation, particles, modality) that enrich or modify the proposition's meaning and truth-conditions.
